analysis.one_liner: Closes royalty loopholes on Gulf oil leases by barring new leases to companies that won't pay royalties at high prices.
analysis.headline: A bill to make Gulf oil companies pay royalties when prices are high died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Some companies holding federal oil and gas leases in the Gulf of Mexico got lease terms that let them drill without paying the government royalties — the public's share of oil taken from federal waters. This bill, sponsored by Rep. Edward Markey, would have barred the Interior Department from issuing any new Gulf leases to a company that refuses to renegotiate those leases so that royalty payments resume once oil and gas prices cross set thresholds (S2, S3). Any royalties collected would go straight to paying down the federal deficit or debt (S2, S3). The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on July 30, 2010 and to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on August 9, and never came back out; it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 (S1, S5).
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would collect royalties on Gulf oil production that would otherwise go unpaid when prices are high, with the money directed to deficit and debt reduction (S2, S3). Future Treasury balances and anyone concerned with the federal debt benefit as well (S2).
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, through oil royalties paid for drilling federal waters.

how_it_helps.text: The bill stops the Interior Department from issuing new Gulf of Mexico oil or gas leases to any company that will not renegotiate existing leases to require royalty payments once oil and gas prices reach specified thresholds (S2, S3).
It blocks companies from sidestepping the requirement by transferring a lease or its benefits to another person (S3).
All royalties and rentals collected are directed to the Treasury to reduce the federal deficit, or the federal debt if there is no deficit (S2, S3).

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding Gulf of Mexico leases with royalty-relief terms: they would owe royalty payments whenever prices reach the thresholds, which lowers the value of those leases (S2, S3).
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies holding royalty-relief Gulf leases.

drawbacks.text: Companies that received royalty relief as part of their original lease terms could argue the bill upends bargained-for contract terms and the value of leases they paid for, and it applies the renegotiation condition only going forward to new leases rather than forcing payment on existing ones (S3).

The bill's remedy is indirect: instead of collecting royalties on existing production, it withholds future new leases from non-complying companies, which could reduce new drilling in the Gulf and, its critics would say, affect domestic oil supply and prices (S2, S3).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public gain is straightforward: royalties on oil taken from federal waters are the government's share, and the bill would have made sure companies pay it when prices are high, with the money going to deficit reduction (S2, S3). The cost falls on leaseholders, who would see the value of price-based royalty relief reduced. The bill addressed only new leases, so it would not have immediately recaptured royalties already being avoided, but it also carried little political cost to the public. On balance, the provisions for ordinary people were larger than the costs they would bear.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee from August 2010 until the Congress ended in January 2011, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on July 30, 2010, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources (S1, S5).
On August 9, 2010, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action followed (S5).
Only four of the House's 253 Democrats signed on as cosponsors, and no Republicans did (S1, S4).
The 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011, and the bill died without ever leaving committee (S1, S5).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding Gulf of Mexico leases with royalty-relief terms are better off: the loophole stayed open because the bill never got a hearing or a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies, which kept royalty-relief lease terms.

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.role: Sponsor; introduced the bill and shepherded it as a committee member
for.what_they_did: Sponsored H.R. 6051 to condition new Gulf leases on royalty-payment renegotiations

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; held the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 30, 2010 and never reported it out; sent it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it remained until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Only 4 of 253 House Democrats cosponsored and no Republicans did, so the bill never drew enough support on either side to force a floor fight; it died quietly in committee (S1, S4).

industries.industry: Oil and gas (Gulf of Mexico leaseholders)
industries.note: The bill would have required companies with royalty-relief Gulf leases to renegotiate so they pay royalties when prices are high, lowering the value of those lease terms. Companies that keep the loophole keep drilling on federal waters without paying the public's share of the resource, so the industry's interest here runs against taxpayers.
Because the bill never became law, the government continues to forgo royalty revenue that the bill would have directed to deficit and debt reduction.
